newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel remembers Rabin amid political divisions.
newsitem.headline: Israel remembers Rabin amid political divisions.

text.p: A divided Israel marked the first anniversary on Thursday of the assassination of Yitzhak Rabin with an impassioned call from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for unity and an emotional graveside ceremony.

"The murder of Yitzhak Rabin must remind us of a basic truth: peace begins at home," said Netanyahu, accused by Rabin's widow of having fostered an atmosphere of hate that led to the Labour prime minister's death.
"The choice before us today is to seal the rift and unite or widen the division and disintegrate," the right-wing leader told a memorial session of parliament.

Israelis marked the Jewish calendar anniversary of Rabin's assassination by a right-wing, religious Jew opposed to his peace policies with the Palestinians as divided politically as they were on the eve of the murder on November 4, 1995.
Two dovish legislators, Dedi Zucker and Dalia Itzik, walked out of the Knesset plenum as Netanyahu got up to speak.

"Mr Netanyahu was directly, personally (part of) the deepest incitement that was directed towards Rabin. He never said 'Sorry, I made a mistake'," Zucker told reporters, referring to the Likud leader's attendance at right-wing rallies at which Rabin was called a traitor.
In Tel Aviv, thousands of people streamed to the public square where Rabin was shot dead a year ago during a peace rally. They lit memorial candles and wept.
Schoolchildren marked the killing in a moment of silence.
Family and Israeli leaders across the political spectrum gathered at the gravesite on Jerusalem's Mount Herzl for a state memorial.
"I want to ask your forgiveness, Grandfather. A year has passed and nothing has changed. It appears nothing has changed," Rabin's grandson Yonatan Ben-Artzi said in a speech at the cemetery.
At Mount Herzl, Leah Rabin spoke on a phone moments before the ceremony began. Israel Television said it was a call from U.S. President Bill Clinton.
But sparring between left and right continued unabated over the peace process Rabin embodied and the fate of Israeli-occupied land.

A procession of religious and right-wing cabinet members -- who took office in June on a platform opposed to Rabin's policies -- laid wreathes on the grave but only family members spoke at the ceremony.
It was in sharp contrast to Rabin's funeral last year which attracted scores of world figures, includin drawn to the man who paid with his life for his peace policies.

Israel Television said on Wednesday Netanyahu and dozens of legislators had received death threats in recent weeks, including opposition leader Shimon Peres, who shared the Nobel prize with Rabin for their 1993 peace deal with the Palestinians.
Netanyahu defeated Peres in elections last May by fewer than 30,000 votes.

Rabin's landmark peace deals with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat made the Israeli leader and former war hero an enemy in the eyes of some right-wing Jews who view the West Bank as land promised to the Jews by God.

"There were calls of 'traitor', 'murderer' -- calls aimed at...murdering his character and in the end, spilling his blood," Peres told the parliamentary session. "But Yitzhak moved forward without surrendering to the pressure, fears, zealots and threats."
The idea that a Jew would murder the prime minister of the Jewish state shocked Israelis but a year later left and right could not even agree on how to commemorate the assassination.

Israel's High Court ruled on Thursday against a petition to make the anniversary a national memorial day after right-wing legislators overruled the initiative in parliament that was put forward by a member of Rabin's Labour party.
Rabin's daughter, Dalia Artzi-Filosof, said the family drew some comfort from the decision to hold a memorial session of parliament.
"For us, at least, it is a small victory," she said.
